phonemes.desc: The nj is a palatalised n — “ny” as in “canyon”; the vowel å as in “or”.
The final ð is the soft “th” of “this” — “NYORTH”. The anglicised “Njord” keeps only the n.
The Old Norse form carries the palatal and the soft ð; the plain anglicisation is a separate lexicon entry.

kin.label: Anglicised

pronunciation.note: The name may be related to the Germanic Nerthus of Tacitus’ Germania — the earth-goddess of the first-century North.

domains.title: The Sea, Wealth, the Vanir Hostage
domains.subtitle: God of the Shore and the Fair Wind
domains.lead: Njǫrðr is the Norse sea-god of the safe shore: the Vanir hostage who chose the sea-cliffs over the mountains, father of Freyr and Freyja, giver of wealth and fair winds to sailors and merchants. He is the gods’ peacemaker — the hostage-exchange that ended the Æsir–Vanir war made him the divine guarantee that treaties hold, and the sea’s temper mirrors his: calm, rich, and implacable when crossed.

cards.name: Lord of the Coast
cards.desc: He rules the sea’s edge and the fair wind — sailors and merchants call on him for safe passage and good trade.

cards.name: The Hostage of Peace
cards.desc: Given to the Æsir to seal the peace with the Vanir; the gods’ own guarantee that oaths bind.

cards.name: Father of the Twins
cards.desc: Freyr and Freyja are his children by his sister — the Vanir marriage-custom the Æsir could not accept.

cards.name: Giver of Wealth
cards.desc: Sea-wealth flows from him — the Norse word for wealth and the sea’s gift are his domain together.

mythology.lead: Njǫrðr’s mythology is the peace-myth: the hostage-exchange that ended the gods’ first war, and the marriage that failed across the divine factions. His two stories — the Æsir–Vanir peace and the nine nights with Skaði — are the Norse pantheon’s domestic politics, and both end in the same lesson: some bonds hold, and some were never possible.

myths.title: The Æsir–Vanir Peace
myths.text: The first war in the world — Æsir against Vanir — ended not in victory but in exchange: Njǫrðr and his children went to the Æsir, and the Vanir received Hœnir and Mímir in return. Snorri notes the exchange’s unevenness (the Vanir beheaded Mímir in disgust) and its durability: Njǫrðr became the Æsir’s own sea-lord, the living treaty between the divine races.

myths.title: The Nine Nights with Skaði
myths.text: Skaði, the ski-goddess, chose her husband by his feet among the veiled gods — she reached for Baldr and got Njǫrðr. Their marriage split on geography: he could not sleep in her mountain halls, where the wolves’ howling kept him from rest; she could not sleep by the sea, where the gulls’ crying drove her mad. Nine nights in each home, then the parting — the gods’ most honest divorce.

myths.title: The Flyting’s Accusations
myths.text: Loki’s taunting catalogue in the gods’ hall accuses Njǫrðr of fathering his children on his own sister — the Vanir custom the Æsir condemned — and of letting the hostage’s price be paid in shame. Njǫrðr’s answer is dignity itself: ‘small harm in a lover, when sisters and husbands are beyond the gods’ borders’ — the hostage’s quiet defense of his people’s ways.

myths.title: The Earth-Before-the-Sea
myths.text: Tacitus’ Germania describes the North’s first-century goddess Nerthus — an earth-deity drawn in a covered wagon, feasted, and drowned in her lake in secret rites. Linguists and historians of religion long ago set Njǫrðr and Nerthus side by side: the same divine name, perhaps, before the sea claimed the land’s share — the gender and the element exchanged across the centuries.

lore.syncretism: The Njǫrðr–Nerthus pair is the classic case of a deity’s sex and element swapped across the sources; and his hostage-role maps onto the comparative pattern of the divine guarantor (the Roman fétiales’ peace-gods). In modern Heathenry he is the Vanir’s standard-bearer, invoked at sea-rites and trade-oaths alike.
lore.culturalLegacy: The nine-nights marriage is the Norse corpus’s most quoted domestic story — the gods’ own lesson that love does not survive incompatible homes. Scandinavia’s coastal placenames keep him; and the modern North’s shipping-prayers, where they survive, address the sea-lord by his name.
lore.extendedMeditation: Njǫrðr: the sea-lord with the soft th ending, restored here in the anglicised plain form while the canonical Norse spelling holds the flagship. The plain name is the sailor’s hail — shouted from a deck, the palatal and the ð were always going to be lost; the lexicon keeps both forms, as the shore keeps both the calm and the storm.
lore.archaeology: The wagon-processions of Tacitus’ Nerthus are mirrored in the North German bog-finds — the Dejbjerg wagon, the peat-preserved carts of the Jutland ritual deposits. Njǫrðr himself leaves no image; the sea and the drowned wagons are his archive.
lore.cult: No surviving temple, but the coastal offering-places of the Viking Age — the boat-graves’ provisions, the beach-cairns — read as his. Modern Heathen blóts at the shore address him for wind and wealth, keeping the old bargain.
lore.iconography: A dignified elder of the sea, sometimes with the ship’s tiller or the fish; in modern art, the calm between wave-crests. His icon is the safe shore — the sea’s edge where wealth lands.
lore.reception: Comparative religion uses the Njǫrðr–Nerthus question as the textbook problem of deity-evidence across genres and centuries; and the nine-nights marriage is the standard citation in studies of mythic divorce. The sea-lord has become, in the modern North, the patron invoked when the old treaties are remembered.
